newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Heavy fighting erupts around Goma, east Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Heavy fighting erupts around Goma, east Zaire.

text.p: Heavy fighting erupted around the eastern Zairean town of Goma on Thursday between rebels and their Hutu foes holed up in the teeming refugee camp of Mugunga.
Mortar, anti-aircraft and heavy machinegun fire rocked the area around the camp about 10 km (six miles) west of the town on Rwanda's border.
Most of the fire appeared to come from the rebel side with controlled and occasional volleys from multi-barrelled rocket launchers on strategic Mount Goma overlooking the area.
But mortar rounds came out of the sprawling camp -- five km (three miles) across -- where thousands of fighters are shielded by hundreds of thousands of Hutu refugees.

The fighting erupted as news broke in Goma that the multinational force being readied to intervene in eastern Zaire will not try to disarm the Hutu fighters when they bring aid to the refugees displaced by a month-long rebellion.

There was no official confirmation from the rebel side but Goma residents said they believed the rebels were trying to take on the Hutu fighters before the arrival of the Canadian-led force, with a powerful U.S. military contingent, in a few days.
"The rebels know they've got a few days to do the job before the force comes in. They're doing it while they've got the chance," one Goma resident told Reuters.
Many more rebels were on the streets early on Thursday. People still moved cautiously, but roadblocks were strengthened and vehicles searched more thoroughly, witnesses said.
The Rwandan Hutu fighters -- ex-soldiers called the FAR and Interahamwe militiamen -- are responsible for the genocide of Tutsis and moderate Hutus in Rwanda in 1994.
The Hutus fear revenge for the genocide and are apparently putting up a last stand at Mugunga. They are telling the rest of the 1.2 million refugees in east Zaire not to go back to Rwanda.
U.N. sources say the fighters have murdered some of the refugees who wanted to go home.
